Dimension the height on the drawing, because the man running the pipe builds what is dimensioned and ignores what is merely intended.

lesson_by_role.owner: Nobody in your street has a vent pipe, so the absence of one looks normal and the presence of one looks like a mistake somebody made. That is the whole of why this gets argued about. The pipe is the cheapest life-safety item in your build, and the only reason it is hard to agree to is that it can be seen from the road.
lesson_by_role.architect: Hidden behind a parapet is where this detail goes to die, and it is a designer who puts it there. A vent works on height and on an open mouth, so a pipe that ends in still air has kept the drawing honest and nothing else. If it cannot be explained by somebody standing in the yard, it gets capped, and the tank goes back to holding its own air.
lesson_by_role.engineer: You will be asked to waive this more often than anything else in IS 2470, and the request always comes from people who will not be standing over the open cover. lesson_by_role.contractor: The vent is the smallest line in the job and the easiest to lose inside a lump sum, so it disappears without anybody deciding to remove it. Nothing in the handover checks for it. Quote it as its own named line and losing it becomes a decision somebody has to make out loud, which is usually enough.
lesson_by_role.maistry: You have smelled the inside of a tank and the men above you have not, which is why this pipe is worth less to them than it is to you. Hydrogen sulphide takes your nose out within seconds at the strength that kills, so the warning you have always relied on stops before the danger does. People standing at the edge afterwards say it did not smell of much.

What you are being asked to approve is a tank that leaks at every joint, described on the sheet by two letters and a rectangle. lesson_by_role.owner: Price and what your relatives already have are the two things that actually decide this, and they usually point the same way. Neither of them asks what shape the tank leaves behind. The material matters far less than the size of hole it allows on top and whether solids leave the tank, and a quote mentions neither.
lesson_by_role.architect: What you write here sets the ceiling on every detail above it, and you will not see any of it built. A ring diameter caps the cover size. One compartment pushes solids out to whatever pit the water soaks away into. Both of those are settled by the word you put beside ST, months before anybody stands on the slab, and nobody on site will read it as a decision you made.
lesson_by_role.engineer: You are not choosing this tank. One arrives on a sheet and you are asked whether it can be signed, and almost any of them can, because the structure is never the problem. lesson_by_role.contractor: Every version of this tank that is quicker for your crew is also harder for the man who has to open it, and those two facts never come up in the same conversation. Rings close a pit in a day. A dividing wall costs you a week you have already priced. Nobody inspects the difference, so the market only pays you for one side of it.
lesson_by_role.maistry: The tank you build is usually the tank the lorry delivered, and that was settled by somebody who is not on site today. You are also the only man here who has opened one of these after twenty years of use. What you know about how a tank empties is the one piece of information on this job that nobody ever asks for.

options.result_append: A slab sealed right across also keeps everything the tank makes. Hydrogen sulphide pools low over the sludge and methane collects at the top, under the concrete, and the man who knocks a hole through that slab is leaning over both of them. Breaking it open does not clear either one.

An opening that size lets almost no air through either. The tank holds hydrogen sulphide low over the sludge and methane up under the slab, and lifting one small cover does not shift them in the few minutes before somebody is told to go down.

A sealed slab also keeps every gas the tank makes. Methane gathers at the top, right under the concrete you are casting tomorrow, and hydrogen sulphide lies low over the sludge. The hole somebody knocks through that slab in twenty years will not vent either of them.
